title: Why Is the Sky Blue but Sunsets Red?
pause_note: 'long' lists the beats (0-based) that are followed by a 1.5 s pause instead of the normal gap, so the picture can play on its own after a key idea.

beats: Why is the sky blue?
And if it's blue all day, why does it turn red at sunset?
It isn't a reflection of the sea.
And it isn't the colour of space. Space is black.
Both colours come from the same sunlight and the same air. The only thing that changes is how much air the light has to cross.
Start with sunlight. It looks white, but it's really a mix of every colour.
Light travels as a wave, and each colour has its own wavelength.
Red waves are long, about seven hundred nanometres from one crest to the next.
Blue waves are shorter, about four hundred and fifty.
In empty space, all the colours travel together in a straight line. Nothing separates them.
Then the light reaches the air.
Air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen molecules.
Each one is more than a thousand times smaller than a wave of light.
When a light wave passes a molecule, it shakes the electrons inside it.
The molecule then sends a little of that light back out, in every direction.
This is called scattering. The light isn't absorbed, and it doesn't change colour. It only changes direction.
But here's the catch. Molecules don't scatter every colour equally.
A shorter wave shakes the electrons faster, and a faster shake sends out far more light.
The rule is steep. Halve the wavelength, and the scattering goes up sixteen times.
So blue light is scattered about six times more strongly than red.
Watch what that does. Send a thousand red photons and a thousand blue ones straight down through the whole atmosphere.
Of the red, fewer than forty are scattered. The rest go straight through.
Of the blue, about two hundred are knocked sideways.
Lord Rayleigh worked this out in eighteen seventy-one, so it's called Rayleigh scattering.
At first, people thought dust was doing it. Later, Einstein showed that the air molecules alone are enough.
Now stand on the ground at midday, and look up, away from the sun.
There's no lamp in that direction. Without air, that patch of sky would be black, as it is on the Moon.
But sunlight is streaming through the air above you.
And the molecules up there are scattering a little of it down toward you.
What they scatter is mostly blue.
It happens in every direction you look. So the whole sky glows blue.
The blue sky is sunlight that took a detour.
Meanwhile, the sun itself still looks almost white.
With the sun overhead, the layer of air is thin. About four fifths of the blue still comes straight through.
Look near the horizon, though, and the blue turns pale.
That light has crossed so much air that it's been scattered again and again. The colours end up mixed back together.
And if you climb higher, there's less air above you to scatter light. The sky darkens, and in space it is black.
But wait. Violet waves are even shorter than blue.
They're scattered nearly ten times more than red. So why isn't the sky violet?
Three reasons. The sun gives off less violet than blue to begin with.
Some of that violet is absorbed high in the atmosphere.
And our eyes are much less sensitive to violet than to blue.
Put those together, and the mix that reaches your brain reads as blue.
Now let the sun go down.
The atmosphere is a thin shell around the Earth. At midday, sunlight takes the short way through it.
At sunset, the light comes in almost flat, skimming along the ground.
That path crosses about thirty-eight times more air.
And every molecule along the way is still doing the same thing: knocking blue out of the beam.
Follow the beam as it goes. It starts out white.
Then it turns yellow, then orange, as the blue and the green drain away.
Over that distance, it adds up. In clean air, less than a thousandth of the blue is left.
But about a quarter of the red survives.
So the sun you see is what's left over: orange and red.
That leftover light paints the clouds and the low sky around it.
Dust and haze in the air can deepen the colour even more.
Sunrise works the same way, with the light skimming in from the east.
So where did the blue from your sunset go?
It wasn't destroyed. Scattered light never vanishes. It only goes somewhere else.
It left the beam along the way, far to the west of you.
Out there, it's still afternoon. And that scattered light is somebody else's blue sky.
The blue sky and the red sunset are two halves of the same sunlight.
The same idea explains clouds. A cloud droplet is much bigger than a wave of light.
Drops that big scatter every colour about equally. So clouds look white.
And on Mars, it works the other way round.
The air there is thin, and full of fine dust. That dust turns the daytime sky orange.
But around the setting sun, the Martian sky glows blue.
So the sky has no colour of its own.
Air scatters blue light far more than red. Look away from the sun, and you see the blue that was scattered.
Look toward a setting sun, and you see the red that wasn't.
Next time you watch a sunset, remember: someone to the west of you is getting your blue.
That's why it does that.
